entry.title: scRNA QC - Short vs Long Read Sequencing

link.title: scRNA QC - Short vs Long Read Sequencing

entry.content:
Project: Compare Sequencing Platforms in Terms of Immune Repertoire Analysis

Sequencing Platforms: Illumina NextSeq short read vs PacBio+Kinnex long read

Assumptions:

Matched sample pairs were analyzed using short-read and long-read single-cell sequencing workflows generated from the same 10x Genomics cDNA libraries (verify the fluorescence intensity and molarity distribution with Bioanalyser). Sequencing libraries passed standard quality control metrics (e.g., PacBio, Table2 [1]; Illumina, Table3 [2]) and comparable analytical tools and workflows were applied for both datasets.

Evaluation of immune receptor recovery across cell types [3]

  • Compare immune cell-type detection between sequencing methods by assessing whether specific populations (e.g., γδ T-cells) are differentially recovered. (PacBio/Kinnex passes if it recovers the same major immune populations without systematic loss of rare cell populations.)

  • Assess full-length paired-chain recovery within detected B-cell (e.g., H/L chains) and T-cell populations (e.g., α/β chains) across clonotypes to evaluate immune receptor reconstruction. (PacBio/Kinnex passes if it achieves higher full-length paired-chain recovery across individual single-cell barcodes.)

Evaluation of platform-dependent differences in recombination profiles and clonal architecture [4]

  • Comparison of V(D)J gene usage and recombination patterns across both BCR and TCR chains, including IGHV vs IGHD, IGHV vs IGHJ, IGKV vs IGKJ, and TRAV vs TRAJ gene combinations. Clonal architecture can also be evaluated using diversity metrics (e.g., Shannon diversity) for each immunoglobulin and T cell receptor chain. (PacBio/Kinnex passes if it yields a denser V(D)J matrix with higher read-count abundance and fewer dropouts (e.g., visualization with heatmap), and if it yields overall higher diversity.)

  • Method-specific and shared recombination patterns can also be summarized. CDR3 structure comparisons can include complete CDR3 recovery rate, CDR3 length distribution and CDR3 motif structure analysis between sequencing methods.(PacBio/Kinnex passes if it shows high proportion of CDR3 recovery rate, unbiased CDR3 length distribution (need more detailed inspection for actual CDR3 length), comparable CDR3 motifs while also capturing hidden sequence variants.)

References:

[1] PacBio. (2023). Kinnex single-cell RNA kit for single-cell isoform sequencing [Application note]. [PacBio](https://www.pacb.com/wp-content/uploads/Application-note-Kinnex-single-cell-RNA-kit-for-single-cell-isoform-sequencing.pdf)

[2] ChromiumTM Single Cell 3’ v2 Libraries -Sequencing Performance on Illumina® NextSeq® 500 Flow Cells. (n.d.). Retrieved from https://assets.ctfassets.net/an68im79xiti/4p3SmrSj1mYMiyyOewQyAW/d98c236816b15cf247990f47a4ae3ac4/CG000085_Technical_Note_Sequencing_Metrics_for_NextSeq_500.pdf)

[3] A comparison of long-read single-cell transcriptomic approaches Scoones, A. L. A., Lan, Y., Utting, C., Pouncey, L., Lister, A., Kudasheva, S., Mehta, N., Irish, N., Swarbreck, D., Gharbi, K., Haerty, W., Cribbs, A. P., Wright, D. J., & Macaulay, I. C. (2025). A comparison of long-read single-cell transcriptomic approaches. [https://doi.org/10.1101/2025.07.03.662955](https://doi.org/10.1101/2025.07.03.662955)

[4] Systematic evaluation of long- and short-read RNA-seq for human peripheral blood Iwabuchi, S., Nasti, A., Okada, H., Takeshita, Y., Sato, T.-A., Urabe, T., Takamura, T., Tamura, T., Tajima, A., Matsubara, K., & Kaneko, S. (2026). Systematic evaluation of long- and short-read RNA-seq for human peripheral blood. NAR Molecular Medicine, 3(1). [https://doi.org/10.1093/narmme/ugag006](https://doi.org/10.1093/narmme/ugag006)

entry.title: Pomodoro App
entry.content:
Aim: Build pomodoro app on Macbook menubar

Features: Adjustable and continuous 30, 45, 60 min study time - 5, 10, 25 min break time and pause option with notification sound.

Requirements: Install SwiftBar app

brew install swiftbar

mkdir -p ~/SwiftBarPlugins

Create python script:

nano ~/SwiftBarPlugins/pomodoro.1s.py

Paste this Python Code into pomodoro.1s.py:

Change the path to your Python location using: which python3

Then run this code on Bash:

chmod +x ~/SwiftBarPlugins/pomodoro.1s.py

Finally, open the SwiftBar app. You will see SwiftBar appear in your MacBook menu bar. Click “Refresh All,” and the label will change to “Pomodoro {Time}”.

entry.title: GitHub Traffic Tracker (>14 days)
entry.content:
Overview

Problem Statement: GitHub provides access to only the past 14 days of repository traffic data. Existing solutions are not designed for the specific output I want.

Solution: This tracker stores daily and cumulative counts for total and unique repository views and clones and store them as a CSV file in your Google Drive.

Note: This tracker is designed for a single repository. A separate tracker should be created for each repository.

What this tracker records

The output CSV includes:

  • Daily total views
  • Daily unique views
  • Daily total clones
  • Daily unique clones
  • Cumulative total views
  • Cumulative unique views
  • Cumulative total clones
  • Cumulative unique clones

Important: GitHub provides only a rolling 14-day traffic window. Therefore, cumulative values must be calculated from the saved daily records, not from GitHub’s 14-day totals.

Step 1: Create a GitHub Personal Access Token (PAT)

Go to:

Settings > Developer Settings > Tokens (classic)

Create a token with the repo scope.

Required permissions:

Metadata and Administration - Read only

Save the token. It will be used later as:

GH_TOKEN

Step 2: Create a Google Service Account and JSON key

Go to the Google Cloud Console.

Create a new project:

  1. Click the navigation menu on the top-left corner.
  2. Select APIs & Services > Enable APIs & Services.
  3. Create a project.
  4. Name your project.
  5. Select the organization. I selected No organization.

Enable the Google Drive API:

  1. Use the search bar at the top.
  2. Search for Google Drive API.
  3. Click on it.
  4. Click Enable.

Create a service account:

  1. Click the navigation menu again.
  2. Select IAM & Admin > Service Accounts.
  3. Click Create Service Account.
  4. Enter a Service Account Name.
  5. Click Create and continue.
  6. Under permissions, select Basic > Editor.
  7. Click Done.

Create the JSON key:

  1. Click the email hyperlink for the service account you just created.
  2. Go to the Keys tab.
  3. Click Add key.
  4. Select Create new key.
  5. Select key type: JSON.
  6. Download the JSON file.

This JSON file will be used later as:

GDRIVE_JSON

Step 3: Create the Google Drive CSV file

Open Google Drive in your browser.

Create or select the folder where you want the CSV file to be saved.

Open the JSON file you downloaded and copy the client_email value.

It should look like this:

name@project-id.iam.gserviceaccount.com

Share the Google Drive folder with that email address and give it Editor permission.

Create a CSV file, for example:

traffic states.csv

Open the CSV file and copy the file ID from the URL.

Example URL:

https://docs.google.com/spreadsheets/d/1sdsN3bo-kX8dsdsrawMI/edit?gid=22392112#gid=22392112

The file ID is this part:

1sdsN3bo-kX8dsdsrawMI

This value will be used in the FILE_ID line of the get_traffic.py script.

Step 4: Add the Python script to your GitHub repository

Go to the GitHub repository that you want to track.

Create a file named:

get_traffic.py

Create this file in the main directory of the repository, not inside a folder.

Before running the script, edit these two lines:

Repository name

Change the REPO line to your repository path.

Example:

REPO = "JaneDoe/WeatherApp"

Google Drive file ID

Change the FILE_ID line to the ID of your Google Drive CSV file.

Example:

FILE_ID = "1sdsN3bo-kX8dsdsrawMI"

Create this folder in your repository:

.github/workflows

Inside that folder, create this file:

daily_traffic.yml

Step 6: Configure GitHub repository secrets

In your GitHub repository, go to:

Settings > Secrets and variables > Actions

Click:

New repository secret

Create the following two secrets.

Secret 1

Name:

GH_TOKEN

Value:

Paste your GitHub Personal Access Token.

Secret 2

Name:

GDRIVE_JSON

Value:

Open your Google Service Account JSON file, copy the entire content, and paste it here.

Step 7: Test the workflow

Go to the Actions tab in your GitHub repository.

Click:

Daily Traffic Sync

Look for this message:

This workflow has a workflow_dispatch event trigger.

Click:

Run workflow > Run workflow

After the workflow finishes, open your Google Drive CSV file and check whether a new row was written.

Done

Your GitHub traffic tracker is now active.

The workflow will run daily and update your CSV file with daily and cumulative repository traffic data.
